outcome: Choi and Lee proved that for each fixed number d of distinct prime divisors, Newman's conjecture holds for a density-1 subset of integers with exactly d distinct prime divisors (extending the reach of the conjecture to almost all multi-prime moduli), with the definitive version appearing as a May 2025 arXiv revision and 2025 publication in Advances in Mathematics; the general conjecture (all moduli) remains open.
summary: The one substantive post-window development on Newman's conjecture is Choi and Lee's paper 'Newman's conjecture for the partition function modulo integers with at least two distinct prime divisors' (arXiv:2212.00636). Its v1 was submitted 1 December 2022 (before the frozen revision date, so not itself a window event), but v2 — submitted 29 May 2025, per the arXiv submission history I fetched directly — carries a changed title and reflects the version that was subsequently accepted and published as Adv. Math. 477 (2025), Paper No. 110367 (DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2025.110367). I treat the May 2025 revision/publication as the dated event under §6.3's rule to date the first written argument that stands behind the eventual public/expert-facing result, since the earlier 2022 preprint was superseded before publication and it was the revised version that was reviewed and published. The paper's main result (its Theorem 1.2, read via the arXiv HTML full text) is that for each fixed d, the density of moduli M with exactly d distinct prime divisors for which Newman's conjecture holds is 1 — a genuine restriction/case of the stated conjecture (moduli with ≥2 distinct prime divisors), not a variant, so it counts as `partial` under §3.1. The triage record's claim that the paper 'explicitly' proves M = 2, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 29, 31 is a misreading I am correcting (§2.2 disagreement): per the arXiv full text, those specific small moduli are prior results due to Newman, Kolberg, Atkin, and Kløve (all well before 2000), cited in Choi-Lee's introduction as background, not new contributions of this paper. I found no acknowledgements section and no mention of any computational or AI tool in the paper (via two independent full-text fetches of the arXiv abstract page and HTML version). Broader searches for any other 2024–2026 work on Newman's conjecture specifically (as opposed to related but distinct partition congruence conjectures, e.g. the 2025 Atkin-O'Brien paper on powers of 13, which is a different named conjecture) turned up nothing else. A generic 2026 arXiv survey on LLMs discovering mathematical conjectures did not mention Newman's conjecture specifically and is not relevant. I therefore find no AI involvement anywhere in the events I could locate for this problem, and no other status-relevant change besides the Choi-Lee result.
competing_reading: One could argue the event should be dated to the original 1 December 2022 submission (making the entire relevant mathematical content pre-window, hence `open_stale`), since the core density-1 argument may not have changed substantively between v1 and v2 — only the title changed, per the arXiv comment field, and the underlying results could already have been complete in 2022. I could not access the full v1 PDF text to diff it against v2 (ScienceDirect returned 403, and I did not separately fetch the v1-only PDF), so I cannot rule out that the mathematical content was unchanged and only journal acceptance/title happened later. If the mathematics itself was unchanged since 2022, `open_stale` would be the more defensible status, since journal publication lag is explicitly excluded from dating under §6.3.
what_would_settle_it: A diff between arXiv v1 (Dec 2022) and v2 (May 2025) full texts, or the Advances in Mathematics referee history, showing whether the density-1 theorem and its proof were already present in v1 or were added/substantially strengthened in the 2025 revision.
